segments.say: Lesson 1. What is System Design. What the interview actually asks, the map of every building block in this app, and the vocabulary (latency, throughput, availability. ) you will use in every answer.

System design is planning how the pieces of a software system (servers, databases, caches, queues) fit together so that it works for many users: fast, reliable, and able to grow. Here is an analogy. Coding is building one great room. System design is planning the whole building: where the entrances go, how many lifts, where water and power run, and what happens if one lift breaks during rush hour.

Why does this matter? Most mid-level and senior interviews include a system design round (often 45–60 minutes). There's no single right answer. They judge how you reason about trade-offs. A few key words. High-level design (H L D): The big boxes and arrows: services, databases, queues. Low-level design (L L D): Classes, A P Is and data models inside one component. Functional requirements: What the system must do (send a message, upload a video). Non-functional requirements: How well it must do it (fast, always up, secure, scalable). Trade-off: Gaining one quality by giving up another.

segments.say: The map: a typical web system. Here is almost every system you'll design. This app teaches each box in its own lesson. First, a one-line tour.

segments.sec: Watch: The map: a typical web system
segments.say: D N S: the internet's phone book, turning app.com into a server's I P address.

segments.sec: Watch: The map: a typical web system
segments.say: C D N: copies of images, videos and J S stored in data centres near users, so they load fast.

segments.sec: Watch: The map: a typical web system
segments.say: Load balancer: the receptionist spreading incoming requests across many servers.

segments.sec: Watch: The map: a typical web system
segments.say: App servers: run your backend code. We run many identical copies so we can handle more users.

segments.sec: Watch: The map: a typical web system
segments.say: Cache: keeps popular data in memory so we don't hit the database every time (~1 ms versus ~10 ms).

segments.sec: Watch: The map: a typical web system
segments.say: Database: where data permanently lives. Choosing and scaling it is often the hardest part.

segments.sec: Watch: The map: a typical web system
segments.say: Queue plus workers: slow jobs (sending emails, processing videos) happen in the background so users don't wait.
Requirements for "Design WhatsApp". Functional requirements equals features. In an interview, agree on 3–4 core ones and explicitly park the rest.
Non-functional requirements equals qualities: speed, reliability, scale, security. These drive the architecture far more than features do.
Every design is a set of trade-offs. Saying "I choose X over Y because. " is what interviewers listen for.

The 6 quality words (use them in every answer). Latency: how long one request takes (ms). Throughput: how many requests per second (Q P S) the system handles. Availability: % of time it works (99.9% about 43 min down a month). Scalability: can it handle 10 times more users by adding machines. Consistency: does everyone see the latest data immediately. Durability: once saved, data is never lost.

What interviewers evaluate. Do you clarify requirements before drawing. Can you produce a working end-to-end design. Do you find the bottlenecks yourself and go deep. Do you explain trade-offs and failure handling. Do you communicate clearly and manage time.

Suggested path through this app. Client/server basics leads to how a request travels leads to scaling leads to load balancers leads to caching leads to databases leads to replication & sharding leads to cap leads to queues leads to A P Is leads to microservices leads to reliability leads to estimation leads to then the 6 classic design rounds.

Say it in the interview. "Before I design anything, let me confirm the core features and the scale. How many users? Read-heavy or write-heavy? What latency and availability do we need? Then I'll sketch a high-level design and we can go deep where you'd like.".

Let's compare. Focus: components and how they connect, classes, methods, schemas inside one component. Typical question: "Design YouTube", "Design a parking lot class model". Artefacts: architecture diagram, data flow, class diagrams, A P Is, D B tables. This app: main focus, touched on in A P I & data model steps.

A likely interview question: What is system design? A strong answer: Planning how components (servers, databases, caches, queues) work together so a system meets its functional requirements and its non-functional ones (latency, scale, availability, consistency), with the trade-offs made explicit.
That's it for What is System Design. Now play the quiz and games in the app to lock it in. See you in the next lesson.
